question: Write a precise definition of a circle. Base it on the notions of point, plane, and distance (you may use ordinary words such as "set", "all", and "given"). Name the center and the radius in your definition.
correct_answer: A circle is the set of all points in a plane that are a given positive distance (the radius) from a given point in that plane (the center).
grading_note: Any equivalent wording. Essential: (1) ALL points, (2) in one plane, (3) at one fixed positive distance, (4) from one fixed point, the center. Not accepted: "a round shape" (not precise); leaving out the plane (that describes a sphere); "points within a distance" (that is a disk).

required_method: Translate A to D; rotate so ray AB lies on ray DE (B lands on E); reflect across DE if needed; then use the two angles to place rays AC and BC on rays DF and EF.
grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: (1) A → D and B → E using AB = DE; (2) C on F's side of DE (reflect if needed); (3) ray AC lands on ray DF because ∠A ≅ ∠D; (4) ray BC lands on ray EF because ∠B ≅ ∠E; (5) C is where rays AC and BC meet, so it lands where DF and EF meet, which is F. Invalid: using side lengths AC or BC (not given); citing ASA to prove ASA.

question: In △ABC, ∠B ≅ ∠C. Let ℓ be the perpendicular bisector of BC. Explain, using the reflection across ℓ and the ASA argument, why the reflection carries △ABC onto △ACB, and conclude that AB = AC.
correct_answer: The reflection swaps B and C, sends ray BA onto ray CA and ray CA onto ray BA, so it fixes A; hence segment AB maps onto AC and AB = AC.

question: A cube with edge s is split into three congruent pyramids that share one vertex of the cube as their apex, as shown. Use this, together with scaling and Cavalieri's principle, to explain why EVERY pyramid with base area B and height h has volume ⅓Bh.

Any pyramid with base area B and height h has cross-sections B((h - y)/h)² at height y, the same as a square pyramid with base area B and height h, so by Cavalieri's principle its volume is ⅓Bh.
required_method: (1) Find the volume of one of the three pyramids. (2) Stretch it vertically to any height h. (3) Use Cavalieri's principle to compare any pyramid with a square pyramid of the same base area and height.
grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: (1) the three congruent pyramids fill the cube, each with base s² and height s, so ⅓s³; (2) a vertical stretch extends this to any height; (3) cross-sections are scaled copies of the base with area B((h - y)/h)², so Cavalieri's principle extends it to any base shape and apex position. The cube case alone is NOT sufficient for full credit.
